prompt.text:
You are working in a copy of the MessagePack-CSharp repository (C#), at the commit just before the change. Solve the problem described below by editing files in this folder.

Rules for this run:
- This machine has no .NET SDK. You cannot build the code or run unit tests. Do not try. Reason from the code.
- Work only inside this folder. Do not use the web. Do not use git.
- When you are done, reply with a short list of the files you changed and why.

How to work:
Solve this the way you normally would for a pull request to this repository. Use your own judgement about what belongs in the change.

## Requirements (from the pull request description)

Requirement: Feature request #2129 in MessagePack-CSharp.

Why: Project A cannot use MessagePack. So Project B needs to make the save-and-load code for Project A's type.

Before and after: Before: no way to do this. After: mark a class with `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` and the code is made for you.

Must preserve: Projects that do not use the new marker must get the same output as before.

## The feature request the Requirement row points to (issue #2129, word for word)

# Feature Request: Allow generation of Formatter for a type in a referenced assembly

## Is your feature request related to a problem? Please describe.

Given the following project structure:

 - Project A
    - `ProjectA.MyType`

 - Project B
    - References
        - Project A
    - Package References
        - MessagePack
    
I need to have a source-generated `IMessagePackFormatter` for type `ProjectA.MyType` generated **inside Project B** instead of Project A, because the latter has no (and cannot have) reference to MessagePack nuget package.

## Describe the solution you'd like

Add a `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` attribute that will work for partial classes implementing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`.

For example:

```csharp
[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
partial class MyObjectFormatter: IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
```

That's it. The class does not even need to declare a body (no `{` and `}`), because the actual implementation is source-generated by `MessagePack.SourceGenerator.MessagePackGenerator` as usual.

As for the attribute-based property keys and other settings (such as Union), I can think of 3 alternatives:

1 - Use `System.Runtime.Serialization.DataMember` and related attributes. This is too limited IMO, as it cannot have `Union` and other features.

2 - Allow the generator and analyzers to work with user-defined versions of the MessagePack attributes. This would be similar to how you can declare dummy versions of BCL attributes that the C# compiler expects, such as [`[IsExternalInit]`](https://stackoverflow.com/a/67687186/643085) or `[ModuleInitializer]`. With this, I could simply copy and paste the attribute definitions for MessagePack attributes such as `[Key]` into my Project A, and have the source-generated formatter (as described above) pick them.

3 - Source-generate the attributes themselves using [`IncrementalGeneratorInitializationContext.RegisterPostInitializationOutput`](https://github.com/dotnet/roslyn/blob/main/docs/features/incremental-generators.md#outputting-values) instead of them existing in the `MessagePack.Annotations` assembly. This would allow using the attributes without adding an additional runtime dependency. Only compile-time reference to the analyzer Nuget would be required.

## Motivation

Project A is really a library (Nuget package), and I really want to keep it minimal. It currently has zero dependencies and I would really like to keep it that way.

runs.reply:
I added `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]`, but nothing has been built or tested, since there's no .NET SDK here. Adding it to a partial class that implements `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` makes the generator write the `Serialize` and `Deserialize` methods into that class.

How it behaves:
- **Which types work:** `T` must be a non-generic class or struct. It can live in a referenced assembly with no MessagePack attributes, because the generator skips the usual metadata and attribute checks for it.
- **How it's serialized:** if `T` has no `[MessagePackObject]`, its public instance members are written as a map keyed by member name. If it does have `[MessagePackObject]`, its attributes apply as usual.
- **Resolver:** the formatter is registered in the generated resolver like any other.
- **Not covered:** generic data types or formatters aren't supported and are silently skipped. Nested types from Project A are not generated automatically, so each one needs its own marked formatter.

Projects that don't use the marker should get the same output as before. Without the marker, `GetObjectInfo` and `ObjectSerializationInfo.Create` behave as they did.

Files changed (paths relative to the repo root):
- `src/MessagePack.Annotations/AnalyzerAttributes.cs`: the new `GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute`, with the same `Conditional("NEVERDEFINED")` pattern as the other analyzer attributes.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Utils/Constants.cs`: the attribute name constant.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/MessagePackGenerator.cs`: a new pipeline input for marked classes. It finds the single `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` on each and collects `T` with that class as the formatter.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs`:
  - The new collection path for the marked formatter.
  - Map mode is forced when `T` has no `[MessagePackObject]`.
  - `contractAttr` is now null-guarded in `GetObjectInfo`.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/ResolverRegisterInfo.cs` and `ObjectSerializationInfo.cs`: a new `FormatterPosition.UserDeclared` value, an `IsFormatterUserDeclared` property, and the formatter name taken from the user's class.
- `FormatterTemplate.tt` and `.cs`, and `StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt` and `.cs`, under `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/`: for a user-declared formatter they emit `partial class Name` with no `internal sealed` and no interface list, since the user already declared it. I edited the generated `.cs` files by hand to match the `.tt` files, so a T4 regeneration may differ slightly in whitespace.
- `README.md`: a short section on the new attribute.

I did not add tests. A generator test in `GenerationTests.cs` would be the natural follow-up once someone can run the build.

+#### Generating a formatter for a type you cannot annotate

 ### MagicOnion
 
 [MagicOnion](https://github.com/Cysharp/MagicOnion) is a code-first gRPC framework based on grpc-dotnet and MessagePack. gRPC usually communicates with Protocol Buffers using IDL. But MagicOnion uses MessagePack for C# and does not need IDL. When communicating C# to C#, schemaless (or rather C# classes as schema) is better than using IDL.

I added `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]`. Nothing was compiled or tested, since there's no .NET SDK here.

Marking a partial class with it, as in `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter] partial class MyObjectFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;`, makes the generator write the `Serialize`/`Deserialize` implementation into that class.

- **How the data type is serialized:** `MyObject` needs no attributes. It is formatted in map mode: every public field and property is written by name, except members marked `IgnoreDataMember`.
- **Limits:** the formatter class must be non-generic. `T` must be an accessible, non-generic class or struct. A formatter that doesn't meet this is skipped without a diagnostic.
- **Private setters:** a public property with a private setter gives a compile error in the generated code. I left this unhandled.
- **Resolver:** the generated formatter is also registered in the source-generated resolver, once.
- **Unchanged output:** projects that don't use the attribute should get the same output as before. The new attribute class is a purely additive public API.

I hand-edited the generated T4 template `.cs` files alongside their `.tt` sources, because I can't run T4 here. The edit is one line in each template.

Files changed:
- [GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.cs](src/MessagePack/GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.cs) is new. It adds the attribute next to the resolver attribute. I added it to the four `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt` files under `src/MessagePack`.
- [Constants.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Utils/Constants.cs) has the attribute name.
- [MessagePackGenerator.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/MessagePackGenerator.cs) finds annotated formatters and works out `T`. It also stops those formatters being registered twice in the resolver.
- [TypeCollector.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs) accepts a user-declared formatter. It treats an unattributed `T` from another assembly as a map-mode object.
- [ObjectSerializationInfo.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/ObjectSerializationInfo.cs) and [ResolverRegisterInfo.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/ResolverRegisterInfo.cs) use the user's class as the formatter. They add a `UserDeclared` position and `FormatterDeclarationModifiers`.
- The two formatter templates, `FormatterTemplate` and `StringKeyFormatterTemplate`, now emit `partial class` for a user-declared formatter. Other formatters still get `internal sealed class`.
- [README.md](README.md) has a short usage section.

I didn't add tests. They need the SDK to run, and I couldn't check them here.

runs.reply:
I added `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]`. I couldn't build or run anything here, so none of it has been compiled or tested, and I added no tests or docs.

When you mark a partial class that implements `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`, the generator now does three things:
- **Formatter for `T`:** it produces the usual formatter for `T`, even when `T` comes from a referenced assembly with no MessagePack attributes.
- **Serialization of `T`:** since `T` can't carry `[MessagePackObject]` or `[Key]`, it is written in map mode. All public instance properties and fields are serialized by name, except ones marked `[Ignore]`/`[IgnoreDataMember]`.
- **Your class:** the generated file fills in `Serialize` and `Deserialize` on your partial class and forwards them to that formatter.

I did this with forwarding because the existing formatter templates are generated from `.tt` files, which I couldn't regenerate here.

**Other behaviour:**
- Your attributed class is left out of the resolver's list of custom formatters. Otherwise `T` would be treated as already handled and nothing would be generated for it.
- Without the marker, nothing changes for existing projects. The new code only runs for a type reached through the attribute, and `Collect` gets an optional trailing parameter that defaults to false.
- If `T` is generic or isn't a class or struct, nothing is generated. You then get the ordinary compile error that your class doesn't implement the interface.

**Files changed:**
- [GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.cs](src/MessagePack/GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.cs): new attribute, conditional like the resolver one.
- `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt` under `src/MessagePack/` for `net8.0`, `netstandard2.1`, `netstandard2.0` and `net472`: the new public API entries.
- [Constants.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Utils/Constants.cs): the attribute name.
- [AnalyzerOptions.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/AnalyzerOptions.cs): the exclusion described above.
- [TypeCollector.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs): lets the target type be collected without `[MessagePackObject]` or when it comes from metadata, and forces map mode for it.
- [MessagePackGenerator.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/MessagePackGenerator.cs): finds the attributed classes, passes `T` to the collector, and registers the extra output.
- [MessagePackGenerator.Emit.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/MessagePackGenerator.Emit.cs): emits the forwarding partial class, including its namespace and any containing types.

I didn't touch the Unity copy of the generator.

+using System;
+using System.Diagnostics;
+
+namespace MessagePack
+{
+    /// <summary>
+    /// An attribute to apply to a <see langword="partial" /> <see langword="class" /> that implements
+    /// <c>IMessagePackFormatter<T></c>, to have the implementation source-generated for <c>T</c>.
+    /// </summary>
+    /// <remarks>
+    /// This is useful when <c>T</c> is declared in an assembly that cannot reference MessagePack.
+    /// Because <c>T</c> cannot be attributed, all its public instance properties and fields are serialized by name in a map,
+    /// except those attributed with <see cref="System.Runtime.Serialization.IgnoreDataMemberAttribute"/>.
+    /// </remarks>
+    [AttributeUsage(System.AttributeTargets.Class, Inherited = false, AllowMultiple = false)]
+    [Conditional("NEVERDEFINED")] // We only need this attribute for source generation, so we don't want it to be included in the user's built assembly.
+    public class GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute : Attribute
+    {
+        /// <summary>
+        /// Initializes a new instance of the <see cref="GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute"/> class.
+        /// </summary>
+        public GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute()
+        {
+        }
+    }
+}

I added `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]`. I couldn't build or run anything here, so none of it is compiled or tested. I added no tests or docs.

You mark a `partial class` that implements `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`. The generator then fills in `Serialize` and `Deserialize` for `T`, including a `T` from a referenced assembly that has no MessagePack attributes. `T` needs no attributes, so it is written in map mode by its public properties and fields. If `T` does carry `[MessagePackObject]`, that attribute is honoured as before.

Projects that don't use the marker should get the same output as before. In both the `.tt` and `.cs` templates, the old class header text is emitted unchanged unless the formatter is user-declared.

Files changed:
- `src/MessagePack/GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.cs` (new): the attribute, conditional like the resolver one.
- `src/MessagePack/*/PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt` (net472, netstandard2.0, netstandard2.1, net8.0): the new public API entries.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Utils/Constants.cs`: the attribute name constant.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/MessagePackGenerator.cs`: a new pipeline that finds attributed classes, takes `T` from the `IMessagePackFormatter<T>` interface and generates the members.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs`: a new `CollectUserFormatter` entry point. A type the user asked a formatter for is collected even without `[MessagePackObject]` or from metadata, using map mode. The `AllowPrivate` diagnostic block now only runs when the attribute is present, which keeps the old behaviour.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/ObjectSerializationInfo.cs`: a new `IsUserDefinedFormatter` flag, included in equality.
- `src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Transforms/FormatterTemplate.{tt,cs}` and `StringKey/StringKeyFormatterTemplate.{tt,cs}`: for a user-declared formatter they emit only `partial class Name`, with no access modifier, base list or constraints. The `.cs` files are generated from the `.tt` files, and I edited both by hand.

Limits:
- The generated formatter is not added to the generated resolver, so you register it yourself, for example through `CompositeResolver` or `[MessagePackFormatter]`.
- Types that `T`'s members refer to are not generated as a side effect, to avoid duplicate output.
- Generic data types are untested.
- I added no analyzer diagnostics for misuse, such as a non-partial class or a missing `IMessagePackFormatter<T>`. Those cases just generate nothing.

+// Copyright (c) All contributors. All rights reserved.
+// Licensed under the MIT license. See LICENSE file in the project root for full license information.
+
+using System;
+using System.Diagnostics;
+
+namespace MessagePack
+{
+    /// <summary>
+    /// An attribute to apply to a <see langword="partial" /> <see langword="class" /> that implements
+    /// <c>IMessagePackFormatter<T></c> to have the Serialize and Deserialize methods source-generated
+    /// for <c>T</c>, which may be declared in a referenced assembly that does not reference MessagePack.
+    /// </summary>
+    /// <remarks>
+    /// Because <c>T</c> cannot be attributed, all its public instance properties and fields are serialized
+    /// in map mode (by name), unless <c>T</c> is attributed with <see cref="MessagePackObjectAttribute"/>.
+    /// </remarks>
+    [AttributeUsage(System.AttributeTargets.Class, Inherited = false, AllowMultiple = false)]
+    [Conditional("NEVERDEFINED")] // We only need this attribute for source generation, so we don't want it to be included in the user's built assembly.
+    public class GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute : Attribute
+    {
+        /// <summary>
+        /// Initializes a new instance of the <see cref="GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute"/> class.
+        /// </summary>
+        public GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute()
+        {
+        }
+    }
+}

`[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]` is implemented. I couldn't build or run anything here, so none of it has been compiled or tested.

I didn't add a generator test. They are snapshot-based and I can't produce the expected `.g.cs` files without running the generator, so that is still to do.

For a type like `partial class MyObjectFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;`, the generator fills in the class body. It serializes all public instance properties and fields of `MyObject` as a map keyed by member name. `MyObject` can live in a referenced assembly and needs no MessagePack attributes. The generated formatter is also registered in the source-generated resolver.

Limits, also noted in the README: the formatter class and the data type must be non-generic, and the data type must be a public class or struct. An unsupported class is skipped silently, with no diagnostic.

Projects that don't use the new attribute should get the same output as before. The templates still write `internal sealed class` unless the formatter is user-declared.

Files changed:
- [GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.cs](src/MessagePack/GeneratedMessagePackFormatterAttribute.cs) is new: the public attribute, with the same pattern as `GeneratedMessagePackResolver`.
- The four `PublicAPI.Unshipped.txt` files under `src/MessagePack/` (net472, net8.0, netstandard2.0, netstandard2.1) list the new public type.
- [Constants.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/Utils/Constants.cs) has the attribute name constant.
- [MessagePackGenerator.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/MessagePackGenerator.cs) finds the attributed classes and feeds each to the type collector. I restructured the combine tuple to carry the extra input.
- [TypeCollector.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/TypeCollector.cs) has a new `CollectForUserFormatter`. For that one type it skips the checks that would otherwise reject a metadata type without `[MessagePackObject]`, and it forces map mode. It then points the resulting info at the user's formatter class.
- [ObjectSerializationInfo.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/ObjectSerializationInfo.cs) gains `IsFormatterUserDeclared` and `FormatterDeclarationModifiers` (`partial` when user-declared, otherwise `internal sealed`).
- `FormatterTemplate.tt` and `.cs`, and `StringKeyFormatterTemplate.tt` and `.cs`, write that modifier string before `class`. I edited the `.cs` files by hand to match the `.tt` files, since I couldn't run the T4 transform.
- [AnalyzerOptions.cs](src/MessagePack.SourceGenerator/CodeAnalysis/AnalyzerOptions.cs) treats the attributed class as excluded from custom-formatter discovery. Otherwise the resolver would register it twice.
- [README.md](README.md) has a short section on the feature under "AOT Code Generation".

@@ -1636,6 +1636,20 @@ Two assembly-level attributes exist to help with mixing in your own custom forma
 
 Learn more about using a mix of your own custom formatters and automatically generated ones in [the Analyzer section](#analyzer).
 
+### Generating a formatter for a type you cannot annotate
+
+A type in another assembly (one that cannot reference MessagePack) cannot carry `[MessagePackObject]`.
+To generate a formatter for it in your own project, declare a `partial` formatter class for the type and apply `[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]`:
+
+```cs
+[GeneratedMessagePackFormatter]
+partial class MyObjectFormatter : IMessagePackFormatter<MyObject>;
+```
+
+The source generator implements the class. All public instance properties and fields of `MyObject` are serialized as a map keyed by member name.
+The formatter class must be non-generic with an accessible default constructor, and the data type must be a non-generic, publicly accessible class or struct.
+The generated formatter is included in the source generated resolver.
+
 ### MagicOnion
 
 [MagicOnion](https://github.com/Cysharp/MagicOnion) is a code-first gRPC framework based on grpc-dotnet and MessagePack. gRPC usually communicates with Protocol Buffers using IDL. But MagicOnion uses MessagePack for C# and does not need IDL. When communicating C# to C#, schemaless (or rather C# classes as schema) is better than using IDL.
